Theme

School & learning

take notes verb

also jot down, note down, take down, notes, note, write down, make notes, classroom commands

classical

Suet. Tit. 3: notīs quoque excipere vēlōcissimē solitum, to take down in shorthand (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 32

excipiō, excipere, excēpī, exceptum

verb, third conjugation (-iō)

take down (what is said)

Catching words as they are spoken, from a lecture or a speaker.

Other words

  • ēnotō, ēnotāre, ēnotāvī, ēnotātum — note down

    verb, first conjugation · classical · Plin. Ep. 1.6.1: meditābar aliquid ēnotābamque (Lewis & Short); Quint. 1.7.27 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 34: take notes, ēnotā (ēnotāte)

    Post-Augustan and rare, says Lewis & Short: Pliny uses it of jotting down what he thought of while out hunting.

  • commentāriōs cōnficere — take notes

    also used · modern · Traupman 30

    Built on commentārius, which in Quintilian (3.6.59) is a pupil’s notes of a lesson (Lewis & Short).

  • annotō, annotāre, annotāvī, annotātum — note down, jot down

    verb, first conjugation · also used · post-classical · Col. 12.3.4 (Lewis & Short): ut meminisset atque adnotāret, quid et quandō et cui dedisset; Traupman 27, 30

    Lewis & Short: only in post-Augustan prose.

  • nota, notae f. — a note, a mark, a written sign

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Traupman 30

  • adnotō, adnotāre, adnotāvī, adnotātum — make a note of, write down

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 3.5.10: liber legēbātur, adnotābātur (Lewis & Short s.v. annotō)

    Lewis & Short prefers the spelling adn-; only in post-Augustan prose.

Examples

  • meditābar aliquid ēnotābamque

    I was thinking something over and noting it downPlin. Ep. 1.6.1 (Lewis & Short s.v. ēnotō)

  • Ēnotā (ēnotāte).

    Take notes.Traupman 34

See also notepad, write, record, comment.
